extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for organizing state executive branches and popular control: ballot simplification, appointment vs election of administrative officers, governor powers and relations with legislature, and trade-offs between centralization and representative deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballot should be so simplified as to concentrate the public attention upon the choice of a few powerful and responsible officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce the number of persons to be voted for to an absolute workable minimum so voters know whom they have selected and can watch them; simplification helps translate public opinion into action and arouses political consciousness. Anti-pattern: elaborate miscellaneous lists of offices that discourage effective public oversight and turn elections into contests over mechanism rather than policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of executive appointment power
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the governor power to appoint executive officials (like department heads) rather than electing purely administrative officers such as auditors, treasurers, and secretaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: administrative officers have little discretionary power in shaping policy and are better appointed to ensure efficient and responsible administration. Example: modelled after the President appointing department heads. Trade-off: concentrates power but increases administrative coherence and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make minor administrative offices appointive
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely administrative county or minor state offices should be appointive rather than elective (except where there is a special reason for election).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: allow county board appointing power to cover county offices except sheriff and prosecuting attorney; in urban areas this reduces the personal/political clutter on ballots. Caveat: rural voters may resist losing traditional voting privileges; reform should consider local contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce frequency and separate timing of elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the separation of county, municipal, state, and national elections and lengthen terms of office to avoid overwhelming voters with long ballots annually or biennially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer terms and separated elections can decrease ballot length without eliminating offices; this can be combined with decreasing elective offices. Purpose: reduce voter bewilderment and allow governors time to master administration. Anti-pattern: too frequent elections that inundate voters with choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit wholesale party nominations/curb expert office-fillers
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate wholesale party nominations and adopt drastically simplified ballots to reduce the ranks of expert office-fillers and extra-legal organizations controlling elective offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany simplification with close legal control and direct nominations in some form to make government more transparent and weaken corrupt slate-making. Expected effect: uncover organizational control and let voters see campaign plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance simplification with representative deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: While simplifying administration is desirable, government should not ignore representative, deliberative functions — large policies affecting liberty and property require deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against extreme simplifications (e.g., commission form) that make government purely business-like and neglect deliberation; such schemes risk long-term failure by sidelining representative debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct primary nomination for candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting party candidates by direct vote of enrolled party members (direct primary) rather than by conventions is an accepted practice in many states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: candidates get on primary ballot by petition signatures; primary winner becomes party's official candidate on general election ticket. Effect: democratizes candidate selection but changes party machinery dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor qualifications and term structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors are typically required to be at least thirty years old, citizens, and residents for specified terms; term lengths vary (two or four years common), with some states limiting successive terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most states set residency and age requirements; twenty-three states had four-year terms and twenty-three had two-year terms (as of the cited data). Trend favors longer terms to allow governors time to learn complex administration. Some states impose term limits or bar holding federal office during term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal powers must be derived from the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A governor's formal powers are those explicitly conferred by the state constitution; a general grant of 'executive power' confers little unless specified elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State courts tend to apply narrow construction to gubernatorial powers (less scope than federal President); assess formal authority by written instrument text rather than broad executive grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of decentralized administrative organization
rubrics_metrics.description: State administrations that are decentralized into many elective and appointive independent officers, commissions, and boards hinder harmonious cooperation and reduce the governor's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: multiple independent elected officers (e.g., treasurer with many board memberships) whom the governor cannot remove; results include lack of coordinated policy and potential appointment of incompetent machine candidates on the ticket to balance a governor's popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing appointing power but with legislative checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appointing power is vested in the governor, it is often shared with the upper house which must consent to appointments and removals, producing staggered, longer terms for appointees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in New York governor plus senate appoints many department heads whose terms often exceed the governor's and who can often be removed only with senate consent; exception: some commissions' members removable by governor alone. Impact: varying degrees of executive control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's investigatory and supervisory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors should have power to require information in writing (sometimes under oath) from officers of the executive department and to appoint committees to investigate any executive office or state institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Montana constitution allows written/oath inquiries and appointing committees; Georgia requires periodic sworn examinations of treasurer and comptroller-general; New York's Moreland act permits departmental investigations. Practical effect: increases central oversight when appointive/removal power is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary suspension and removal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors may be given power to temporarily suspend certain state officers during legislative recesses and, in some cases, to remove certain officials (often subject to legislative consent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York governor may temporarily suspend treasurer pending investigation; removal powers and requirements vary by state and office. Anti-pattern: inability to remove malfeasant officers easily leads to administrative paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief and emergency powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors are commander-in-chief of state armed forces and may call out the militia, declare martial law in severe disorders, and (in many states) suspend the writ of habeas corpus in rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two states (and Oklahoma, at time of writing) forbid suspension of habeas corpus by state authorities; emergency powers are significant but constrained by constitutions and judicial review. Use caution: such powers are exceptional and potentially controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's legislative relations and budget role
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors should have the duty to communicate with the legislature, recommend measures, present the state of the commonwealth, and in some states propose the budget; they may call special sessions and, with veto powers (sometimes of single appropriation items), influence legislative priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governor's message can present issues to the people; calling special sessions can force legislative action on prioritized measures. Example: nine states require the governor to propose the budget and many governors have item veto power on appropriations, strengthening fiscal influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and constitutional specification of salary
rubrics_metrics.description: A governor's salary may be fixed by the constitution or left to the legislature; many states pay $5,000 or more (historical data cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York fixed compensation at $10,000 and required the legislature to provide a suitable executive residence. Compensation mechanisms affect independence and attractiveness of office.
